h1:
Pattani Central Mosque
Green dome by a reflecting pool, Pattani's signature landmark
intro: Pattani Central Mosque is the landmark most people picture first when they think of Pattani. The building is a large green-domed structure in Islamic architectural style, fronted by a rectangular reflecting pool that mirrors the mosque on its surface — earning it the nickname "Thailand's Taj Mahal" among many visitors. It was completed in 1963 and has long served as the spiritual heart of the local Muslim community. This page covers everything from the architecture and the best reflection photo spots, to its role as the province's spiritual center, to detailed visiting etiquette — dress code, removing shoes, prayer times to avoid, halal food around the mosque, and how to pair it with Krue Se Mosque and the old town for a full trip.

blocks.html:
Pattani is a southern border province where Muslim culture forms the foundation of local life, and if there's one single image that represents the province, most people would point to Pattani Central Mosque. The mosque sits on Yarang Road in downtown Pattani and is one of the most famous and beautiful provincial mosques in the South. Its green dome stands out sharply against the sky, and in front stretches a long reflecting pool that mirrors the mosque on the water's surface — a photo spot that almost every visitor stops to capture.

Beyond its beauty, Pattani Central Mosque is a hub of faith and religious activity for the local Muslim community — daily prayers, Friday prayers, and important religious events all happen here. This page walks through it point by point, honestly, covering both what impresses visitors and what you should understand before you go, especially the visiting etiquette, because this is a working religious site, not just a photo destination.

blocks.descHtml:
The heart of this landmark is the mosque building itself, in Islamic architectural style — a large green central dome flanked by smaller domes and two tall minarets, with walls decorated in Islamic patterns and arched doorways. What sets it apart from an ordinary mosque is what's in front: a long rectangular reflecting pool stretching out before the building. On a clear day, when the water surface is still, it mirrors the dome and minarets in a beautifully symmetrical image — which is exactly why people compare it to India's Taj Mahal. The most popular photo spot is standing at the far end of the pool, framing the mosque together with its full reflection in one shot. Morning and evening, when the sun is soft and the water is calm, give you the most beautiful shots.

Beyond its beauty, Pattani Central Mosque is the spiritual center of the province — a working provincial mosque where the local Muslim community genuinely practices their faith every day, from the five daily prayers to the large Friday gathering to important religious occasions throughout the year. Visiting here is a chance to experience the way of life and culture of Muslims in the southern border region up close — not just a stop for photos and a quick exit. Visitors should keep in mind that they are guests at someone else's place of worship, so conducting yourself politely and respecting the site matters most of all.

There's quite a bit of visiting etiquette worth knowing before you go. First is dress — dress modestly and cover up, avoiding sleeveless tops, tank tops, and shorts or skirts above the knee; women should bring a headscarf to cover their hair (a hijab or a shawl that can be wrapped over the head) when entering the mosque grounds. Second, always remove your shoes before entering the building. Third, avoid prayer times, especially the Friday midday prayer, since that's when worshippers are using the space and visitors shouldn't disturb them. In general, the mosque does not open its interior to tourists on Fridays, since it's the day of the main weekly prayer — plan to visit on another day instead. If you're not Muslim, some interior areas may be reserved for worshippers only, so ask staff or check posted signs and follow their guidance. Also speak quietly, avoid raising your voice, and ask permission before photographing people who are praying.
blocks.tipHtml: Tip: Dress modestly and cover up, women should bring a headscarf, and remove your shoes before entering the building. Go in the morning or evening when the sun is soft and the water is calm for the best reflection shots. Avoid Fridays, the main weekly prayer day when the mosque usually doesn't open its interior to tourists, and avoid prayer times throughout the day. Pair the trip with Krue Se Mosque (Pattani's other historic brick mosque) and a walk through Pattani's old town, which has old buildings and halal food stalls, for a full dose of architecture, history, and food in one trip.

blocks.title: Know Before You Go: Pattani Central Mosque

items.title: Dress modestly, women cover their hair
items.text: Dress modestly and cover up — no sleeveless tops, tank tops, or shorts/skirts above the knee. Women should bring a headscarf to cover their hair when entering the mosque grounds, out of respect for the religious site.

items.title: Remove your shoes before entering
items.text: Always remove your shoes before entering the mosque building. Leave them at the designated spots, keep your voice down, and walk respectfully within the grounds.

items.title: Avoid prayer times and Fridays
items.text: Avoid prayer times each day, especially Friday, the main weekly prayer day, when the mosque usually doesn't open its interior to tourists. Choose another day to visit, and photograph the exterior respectfully.

items.title: Reflection shots and good light
items.text: The most popular spot is standing at the far end of the pool, framing the mosque with its full reflection. Morning and evening, when the sun is soft and the water is calm, give the most beautiful symmetrical shots — and ask permission before photographing anyone who is praying.

faq.q: Is Pattani Central Mosque free to enter, and can I go inside?
faq.a: Entry is free, no admission fee. Visitors can view the exterior and take reflection photos by the pool. For the interior, dress modestly, remove your shoes, and follow the etiquette of the religious site. Some interior areas may be reserved for worshippers only, so ask staff or check posted signs and follow their guidance.

faq.q: How should I dress to visit Pattani Central Mosque?
faq.a: Dress modestly and cover up, avoiding sleeveless tops, tank tops, and shorts or skirts above the knee. Women should bring a headscarf to cover their hair when entering the mosque grounds, and everyone must remove their shoes before entering the building, since this is a religious site actively used for worship.

faq.q: Why shouldn't I visit on a Friday?
faq.a: Friday is the main weekly prayer day for Muslims, and the mosque will have a large number of worshippers. It generally doesn't open its interior to tourists that day, so plan to visit on another day. On any day, avoid prayer times so as not to disturb worshippers.

faq.q: What time of day is best, and where's the best spot for the reflection photo?
faq.a: Morning or evening is best, when the sun is soft and the water is calm. The most popular spot is standing at the far end of the pool facing the mosque, framing the building together with its full reflection in one shot for the symmetrical image that earns it the nickname Thailand's Taj Mahal. Ask permission before photographing anyone who is praying.

faq.q: What can I pair a visit to Pattani Central Mosque with?
faq.a: Pair it with Krue Se Mosque, a historic brick mosque and an important ancient site in Pattani, then walk through Pattani's old town, which has old buildings and halal restaurants. The area around the mosque and downtown is a Muslim community, so it's easy to find khao yam, nasi dagang, roti, and local sweets. You can cover it all in half a day to a full day.
